headline: Flood each newly discovered land component
statement: Given a rectangular grid of characters 1 for land and 0 for water, count islands. Land cells belong to the same island when joined horizontally or vertically; diagonal contact does not connect islands. Grid boundaries are surrounded by water. The reference may change land to water to mark visited cells; preserving the input with separate visited state is also valid.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
constraints: Every cell is the character "0" or "1".
intuition: Find a land cell that has not yet been counted, then visit all land connected to it. That whole group is one island. Mark cells as you visit them so the next scan does not count the group again. Only cells sharing a side connect; diagonal contact is not enough.
approach: For each remaining 1, increment islands, mark it 0, and enqueue it.
Expand the queue through valid four-direction land neighbors.
Mark a neighbor before enqueueing to prevent duplicate visits.
correctness: Flooding reaches precisely the land connected to the starting cell by four-direction paths. Marking all reached cells prevents recounting that component. Every component has a first scanned land cell, so each island contributes exactly one increment and none are missed.
bruteForce: For each cell, independently search its component and deduplicate component identities afterward. Repeated floods can become quadratic.

complexity.explanation: Each cell is scanned once and land is queued once. The explicit flood queue can hold a linear number of cells; input is mutated to mark visitation.

pitfalls: Use four directions; diagonals are not connected.
Mark when enqueueing rather than when popping.
Characters "1" and "0" differ from integers 1 and 0.
